2352-30421362026NovGenes & diseasesGenes DisTherapeutic resistance in cancer: lncRNAs as modulators and targets for cancer therapy.10199010199010199010.1016/j.gendis.2025.101990Therapeutic resistance continues to be a significant challenge in cancer treatment, often leading to tumor recurrence, metastasis, and limited therapeutic efficacy despite advancements in chemotherapy and radiotherapy. This resistance arises from complex molecular mechanisms that are influenced by various factors, including genetic alterations, epigenetic modifications, and cellular signaling. Recently, lncRNAs, a subclass of non-coding RNAs, have gained prominence for their essential role in driving cancer progression and mediating resistance to therapy. The resistance phenotype is shaped by lncRNAs through the regulation of key signaling pathways, DNA repair mechanisms, and cellular survival processes. For example, lncRNAs such as HOTAIR and MALAT1 are involved in the regulation of PI3K/AKT, EMT, and DNA repair pathways, and influence cell proliferation, apoptosis, and metastasis. These findings underscore the potential of lncRNAs as therapeutic targets. Targeting lncRNA-mediated pathways offers a promising approach to overcome resistance and enhance the efficacy of existing therapies. This review provides an in-depth analysis of the molecular mechanisms by which lncRNAs mediate resistance in various cancers, such as gastric cancer, lung cancer, breast cancer, and hepatocellular carcinoma. 1618-06233122026NovMicrobiological researchMicrobiol ResStructural and molecular insights into Helicobacter pylori CagA-SHP2 complex: From pathogenic signaling to targeted therapeutic opportunities in gastric cancer.12863212863210.1016/j.micres.2026.128632S0944-5013(26)00196-5Gastric cancer (GC) remains a major global health burden, ranking as the fifth most common malignancy worldwide. Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) is strongly implicated in gastric carcinogenesis and was classified as a Class 1 carcinogen by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 1994. Among H. pylori virulence factors, cytotoxin-associated gene A (CagA) plays a pivotal oncogenic role by modulating host signaling pathways through highly specialized molecular interactions utilizing the CagA multimerization (CM) and EPIYA motifs. Following translocation into gastric epithelial cells (GECs) via the type IV secretion system (T4SS), tyrosine phosphorylation at EPIYA motifs ensures aberrant interaction between CagA and the host Src homology 2 domain-containing phosphatase 2 (SHP2). This interaction represents a unique host-pathogen crosstalk mechanism that functionally mimics oncogenic PTPN11 gain-of-function mutations, resulting in sustained activation of MAPK/ERK and focal adhesion kinase (FAK) pathways, cytoskeletal reorganization, increased cellular motility, and the characteristic hummingbird phenotype. This review aims to summarize current knowledge on the structural and functional interplay between CagA and SHP2 and its role in gastric carcinogenesis, while broadly addressing how geographic diversity in CagA variants shapes the interaction and its consequences. It further discusses the broader oncogenic impact of CagA-driven signaling alterations, including emerging evidence for a hit-and-run oncogenic mechanism, and their relevance to disease progression and prevention strategies. The CagA-SHP2 axis emerges as a central pathogenic hub in H. pylori-associated gastric carcinogenesis and an attractive pharmacological target for the development of mechanism-based therapeutic strategies for the disease.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier GmbH. In this study, KAT6A was strikingly upregulated in both gastric cancer tissues and cell lines and was significantly associated with malignant phenotypes and shorter survival periods. We have demonstrated that KAT6A upregulates acetylated histone levels, thereby increasing the transcriptional activity of genes, including HK2, PDL1, and CD47. This consequently promotes elevated glycolytic flux and facilitates immune evasion. Notably, for the first time, we discovered that DEK plays a crucial synergistic role in the activation of H3K27ac by KAT6A and that the knockout of DEK can rescue the related effects of overexpressing KAT6A. 1432-108436112026NovEuropean radiologyEur RadiolSpectral CT-based habitat analysis for predicting pathologic response to neoadjuvant therapy in gastric cancer.824982638249-826310.1007/s00330-026-12727-wTo investigate the predictive value of habitat imaging based on spectral CT-derived iodine maps (IMs) for pathologic response to neoadjuvant therapy (NAT) in gastric cancer (GC).This retrospective, two-center study included 151 patients with pathologically confirmed GC who underwent NAT followed by gastrectomy between July 2022 and June 2025. All patients underwent dual-phase, contrast-enhanced, dual-layer spectral CT scans before NAT. Based on tumor regression grade, patients were categorized as responders or non-responders. In venous-phase IMs, tumor voxels in the entire lesion were clustered into distinct habitats using the k-means algorithm. The volume fraction of each habitat and an intratumoral heterogeneity score (ITHscore) were calculated. Univariate analysis and logistic regression analyses determined predictive parameters among clinicopathologic and IM-based variables. A weighted logistic regression model for responders was developed and validated using fivefold cross-validation and an external test set.Among the 151 patients, 54 (35.8%) were responders. Three distinct perfusion habitats (high, middle, and low) were identified. Responders exhibited a higher volume fraction of the low-perfusion habitat and a lower ITHscore (both p < 0.05). By integrating these two metrics, patients were stratified into four perfusion subtypes, with response rates ranging from 75.0% to 17.4% (p < 0.001). The predictive model combining perfusion subtype and Lauren classification achieved an average area under the curve (AUC) of 0.794 (0.751-0.836) in internal cross-validation and 0.782 (0.605-0.909) in the external test set.IM-derived habitat imaging can distinguish distinct perfusion subtypes, suggesting a promising approach for predicting pathologic response to NAT in GC.Question Accurately predicting the efficacy of neoadjuvant therapy prior to treatment in gastric cancer remains challenging due to the lack of reliable biomarkers. Findings Perfusion subtypes identified through iodine map-based habitat imaging effectively predict tumor regression in gastric cancer following neoadjuvant therapy. Clinical relevance Iodine map-based habitat imaging is a promising biomarker for noninvasively predicting pathologic response to neoadjuvant therapy in patients with gastric cancer, thereby enabling more personalized treatment strategies for this population.© 2026. 1532-30721032026NovTissue & cellTissue CellSENP1 drives glycolytic reprogramming to promote malignant progression of gastric cancer via deSUMOylation of HIF-1α.10370310370310.1016/j.tice.2026.103703S0040-8166(26)00397-6Sentrin/SUMO-specific protease 1 (SENP1), a key deSUMOylating enzyme, stabilizes hypoxia-inducible factor 1-alpha (HIF-1α) to promote tumor aerobic glycolysis. This study aims to determine whether SENP1 drives malignant progression in gastric cancer (GC) through glycolytic reprogramming.SENP1 and HIF-1α expression levels and their association with patient prognosis were analyzed using the GEPIA2.0 database. Clinical GC tissues were collected, and mRNA/protein expression levels were measured. SENP1 knockdown and overexpression models were established. Malignant phenotypes and glycolytic flux were assessed. SENP1-HIF-1α interaction and SUMOylation levels were determined. A subcutaneous xenograft model in nude mice was used for in vivo validation.SENP1 was upregulated in GC tissues and correlated with poor overall survival. SENP1 knockdown suppressed GC cell proliferation, colony formation, migration, and invasion, while promoting apoptosis. Conversely, SENP1 overexpression exerted opposing effects. Moreover, SENP1 depletion reduced glycolytic activity, as indicated by decreased glucose uptake, lactate release, ATP content, and expression of key glycolytic genes. Treatment with DMOG, which stabilizes HIF-1α, partially restored glycolytic activity and mitigated the malignant phenotypes driven by SENP1 knockdown. In vivo, SENP1 silencing impeded tumor growth and downregulated expression of HIF-1α, Ki-67, and key glycolytic genes.SENP1 may de‑SUMOylate HIF-1α, thereby driving glycolysis and malignant progression in GC cells. 1879-355X12632026Nov01International journal of radiation oncology, biology, physicsInt J Radiat Oncol Biol PhysConsolidative Camrelizumab Following Definitive Concurrent Chemoradiation Therapy With Involved-Field Irradiation in Locally Advanced Esophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma: A Single-Arm Phase 2 Trial.672686672-68610.1016/j.ijrobp.2026.04.026S0360-3016(26)00601-2Definitive concurrent chemoradiation therapy (dCCRT) is considered the standard treatment for locally advanced unresectable esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC). However, approximately half of the patients still experience local recurrence or distant metastasis. The CheckMate 577 trial, a phase III randomized clinical trial evaluating adjuvant nivolumab after neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy and surgery, demonstrated that adjuvant nivolumab significantly improves disease-free survival in patients with resected esophageal or gastroesophageal junction cancer after neoadjuvant chemoradiation therapy. However, the role of consolidation immunotherapy in locally advanced unresectable esophageal cancer remains unclear. Camrelizumab, an anti-programmed death receptor 1 antibody, has shown antitumor activity in advanced or metastatic ESCC. We conducted a clinical trial to evaluate the efficacy of camrelizumab consolidation therapy in patients with unresectable, locally advanced ESCC following dCCRT.This single-arm, phase 2 trial was conducted at the Fourth Hospital of Hebei Medical University (Shijiazhuang, China). Eligible patients were aged 18 to 75 years with histopathologically confirmed, locally advanced (T1bN+M0, T2-4N0-2M0, or supraclavicular lymph node metastasis) unresectable or medically inoperable ESCC, who had not experienced disease progression after completing dCCRT. Patients received camrelizumab consolidation therapy (200 mg intravenously, day 1, every 2 weeks) for 12 months. After 12 months, patients could independently choose to continue immunotherapy. The primary endpoint was progression-free survival (PFS). Secondary endpoints included disease control rate, objective response rate, duration of response, overall survival (OS), and safety.Between April 2020 and November 2023, 43 patients were screened, 35 were enrolled, and 32 were included in the analysis. As of the data cutoff date (July 25, 2025), 12 patients had experienced disease progression, and 10 patients had died. The disease control rate was 59.4% (19 of 32). Neither the median PFS nor the median OS was reached. The 1-year, 2-year, and 3-year PFS rates were 81.3%, 62.5%, and 62.5%, respectively. The 1-year, 2-year, and 3-year OS rates were 96.9%, 77.7%, and 63.0%, respectively. Regarding safety, most adverse events (AEs) were grade 1 or 2. The most common AEs were anemia (68.8%), leukopenia (50.0%), and reactive cutaneous capillary endothelial proliferation (43.8%). Grade 3 AEs included leukopenia (12.5%) and thrombocytopenia (3.1%). No treatment-related deaths occurred. 1872-79806592026Oct28Cancer lettersCancer LettIL-15 superagonists for reprogramming the immunosuppressive microenvironment in gastrointestinal adenocarcinomas.21878021878010.1016/j.canlet.2026.218780S0304-3835(26)00544-6Gastrointestinal (GI) adenocarcinomas pose a significant therapeutic challenge due to highly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironments that limit effective antitumor immune responses. Dense stromal fibrosis, immune exclusion and poor responses to immune checkpoint inhibitors are hallmarks of treatment-resistant malignancies, most notably pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) and subsets of gastric cancer. In this regard, IL-15 superagonists such as N-803, NIZ985, RLI, and NKTR-255 have emerged as promising immunotherapeutic candidates, as they selectively expand natural killer (NK) cells and CD8+ T-cells without the systemic toxicity and regulatory T-cell activation observed with IL-2 therapy. IL-15 superagonists have emerged as more effective therapeutic agents when used in conjunction with local inhibitors of TGF-β and IL-10, stromal remodeling, and vascular normalization. They are supported by increasingly conclusive mechanistic, preclinical and early clinical data. A combination of these interventions circumvents extracellular matrix-provoked immune barriers, reverses VEGF-induced endothelial dysfunction, and enhances the trafficking of lymphocytes into tumor cores. Moreover, several localized therapeutic delivery strategies, such as endoscopic delivery, implantable depots, biomaterial scaffolds, and nanocarriers, can improve intratumoral cytokine retention and reduce systemic inflammatory toxicity. Together, these advances define a new paradigm for cytokine-immunotherapy: IL-15 superagonists serving as key mediators of reprogramming of the tumor microenvironment. Therapeutic strategies targeting IL-15 have the potential to restore cytotoxic immunity, improve access to immune cells, and promote responsiveness to the checkpoint blockade, making them a promising yet investigational approach to converting immune-cold GI malignancies into more treatment-responsive disease states, though further clinical validation is required.Copyright © 2026 The Authors. 1872-79806592026Oct28Cancer lettersCancer LettPharmacologic inhibition of SOX9-CDK4 by CYD-4-61 impairs gastric adenocarcinoma growth and amplifies anti-PD-1 response.21877721877710.1016/j.canlet.2026.218777S0304-3835(26)00541-0Gastric adenocarcinoma (GAC) remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality, particularly in patients with peritoneal carcinomatosis, for whom effective therapies are limited. We investigated the therapeutic efficacy and molecular mechanism of CYD-4-61, a BAX activator, using human GAC cell lines, patient-derived xenograft models, genetically engineered mouse models, and a syngeneic mouse model. CYD-4-61 potently inhibited tumor cell proliferation, induced apoptosis, and suppressed cancer stem cell-like properties, with enhanced activity in radiation-resistant GAC cells. Mechanistically, CYD-4-61 activated the BAX-caspase pathway, leading to SOX9 protein reduction. Integrated bulk and single-cell transcriptomic analyses identified SOX9-dependent transcriptional programs as major targets of CYD-4-61. Functional rescue experiments together with chromatin immunoprecipitation and CUT&RUN analyses supported CDK4 as a SOX9-regulated gene and demonstrated suppression of the SOX9-CDK4 regulatory axis following CYD-4-61 treatment. In multiple preclinical models, CYD-4-61 significantly inhibited tumor growth and improved the therapeutic response to anti-programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) therapy while modulating the tumor immune microenvironment. Clinically, co-expression of SOX9 and CDK4 was associated with diffuse-type GAC and poor patient outcomes. These findings identify the BAX-SOX9-CDK4 axis as an important mechanism contributing to the antitumor activity of CYD-4-61 and provide a strong preclinical rationale for its further development as a therapeutic strategy for aggressive GAC.Copyright © 2026 The Authors. A 23 factorial-design (RStudio-v4.3.3) was used to optimize microenvironmental pH, floating lag time (FLT) and drug release. We retrospectively identified patients who underwent radical gastrectomy between January 2015 and October 2025. The primary comparison included 54 patients who underwent RG and 162 who underwent Laparoscopic gastrectomy (LG). After exclusion of patients with missing propensity-score covariates, 53 RG and 143 LG patients were eligible for matching. One-to-two nearest-neighbor matching was performed using a caliper of 0.2 standard deviations of the logit of the propensity score, yielding 45 RG and 88 LG patients. The principal outcomes was the number of lymph nodes retrieved. After matching, all included covariates were balanced. The median number of lymph nodes retrieved did not differ significantly between RG and LG (30 [interquartile range, 25-42] vs 34 [27-47]; 95% Confidence Interval [CI]: -10.0-2.0, p = 0.181). RG was associated with a shorter postoperative length of stay (16 vs 18 days; 95% CI: -4.1-0.1, p = 0.016) and fewer positive lymph nodes (0 vs 2; 95% CI: -3.3-0.7, p = 0.007). Median operative time was 310 minutes for RG and 300 minutes for LG (95% CI: -20.5-40.5, p = 0.072). CUSUM analysis revealed a V-shaped recovery for LN retrieval, and confirmed operative efficiency convergence to the LG benchmark by the late phase (300 min, p = 0.053), together indicating a trend toward improved performance during the learning process. RG and LG achieved comparable lymph-node yields, while RG was associated with a shorter postoperative hospital stay. Exploratory sequential analyses suggested improvement in operative efficiency but did not establish a proficiency threshold. 1573-72334542026Oct17Cancer metastasis reviewsCancer Metastasis RevVascular plasticity in the gastric cancer environment: mechanisms, prognostic significance, and concepts of therapeutic interventions.7610.1007/s10555-026-10388-1Gastric cancer (GC) remains a major global health problem because of its aggressive behavior and frequent development of therapeutic resistance. In GC, as in other malignancies, blood vessels are essential for Tumor-cell survival and dissemination, thereby facilitating metastasis to distant organs. As tumors grow, they remodel the surrounding microenvironment, generating hypoxic, acidic, nutrient-poor conditions with elevated interstitial fluid pressure. Reactive oxygen species further support tumor growth, glycolytic metabolism, and neovascularization. Highly aggressive cancer cells can also form endothelial cell-independent vascular-like networks defined as vasculogenic mimicry (VM), which may facilitate access to oxygen and nutrients. Many molecular markers and mechanisms underlying VM in GC remain insufficiently defined, while the presence of VM is associated with aggressive tumor behavior, metastatic potential, therapeutic resistance, and poor prognosis. Therefore, new therapeutic strategies are needed that complement conventional treatment and target the heterogeneous vascular compartments of GC. Nanomedicine may contribute to this goal by improving targeted drug delivery, local drug concentration, bioavailability, and controlled release while reducing systemic adverse effects.© 2026. 1867-108X2026Oct17Japanese journal of radiologyJpn J RadiolPalliative radiotherapy for gastric cancer-related bleeding: a systematic review and meta-analysis of bleeding response and dose-response relationships.10.1007/s11604-026-02094-3Palliative radiotherapy is commonly used to control bleeding in advanced gastric cancer; however, the optimal dose-fractionation regimen as well as the dose-response relationship remain unclear. We aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of radiotherapy for gastric cancer-related bleeding and its association with dose fractionation.We systematically searched PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, and Ichushi-Web for studies published between January 2000 and August 2026 on palliative radiotherapy for gastric cancer-related bleeding. The primary endpoint was bleeding response rate. A random-effects meta-analysis was performed to estimate the pooled response rates. Meta-regression and subgroup analyses were conducted to explore dose-response relationships. Meta-regression was performed using study-level median biologically effective dose (BED) values.A total of 31 studies were included. The pooled bleeding response rate was 75.9% (95% confidence interval, 69.7-81.2), with significant heterogeneity (I2 = 67.5%). Egger's test suggested small study effects (P = 0.012). Meta-regression analysis demonstrated an association between a higher BED and an increased likelihood of response (P = 0.010). Subgroup analyses showed that higher BED categories were associated with higher response rates (P = 0.005). The pooled rebleeding rate was 32.4%. The median overall survival and rebleeding-free survival were 3.8 and 3.4 months, respectively. Radiotherapy was generally well tolerated, with a low incidence of grade ≥ 3 toxicities.Palliative radiotherapy is an effective and well-tolerated treatment for gastric cancer-related bleeding. Although study-level meta-regression identified a statistical association between higher BED and hemostatic response, this may largely reflect selection bias and methodological limitations rather than a true dose-response relationship. Given the poor prognosis of this population, shorter dose-fractionation regimens are appropriate for many patients, whereas higher-BED regimens remain reasonable for selected patients.© 2026. 1432-19122026Oct17Naunyn-Schmiedeberg's archives of pharmacologyNaunyn Schmiedebergs Arch PharmacolIdentification of a novel Microbacterium species and biosynthesis of gold nanoparticles: activation of apoptosis and dysregulation of ABCG transporters in gastric adenocarcinoma cells.10.1007/s00210-026-06011-3Gastric cancer has high morbidity and mortality rates worldwide, often requiring new therapeutic approaches. Biosynthesis of gold nanoparticles (GNPs) offers a promising treatment due to their unique biological properties and biocompatibility. In this study, we synthesized gold nanoparticles using the cultural supernatant of Microbacterium sp. MAH-37 (MM37-S) and evaluated their anti-gastric cancer activity, focusing on apoptosis induction and regulation of the ABCG transporter pathway. The Microbacterium sp. strain MAH-37 was isolated from pumpkin garden soil, and its morphology was characterized by transmission electron microscopy (TEM). The successful biosynthesis of MM37-S-GNP was confirmed by UV-visible spectroscopy, SAED, DLS, FTIR, XRD, EDX, and FE-TEM analyses. Biological evaluations revealed that MM37-S-GNPs exhibited cytotoxicity of approximately 72% at 200 µg/mL against AGS cells and confirmed by colony formation and Live/Dead assay, whereas normal HFE-145 cells was non-toxic. Furthermore, Hoechst 33,258, propidium iodide, and Mito Tracker revealed nuclear condensation and fragmentation, membrane-compromised cells, and mitochondrial disruption, respectively, indicating cell death via apoptosis. H2DCFDA staining demonstrated a significant increase intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation in AGS cells following MM37-S-GNP. Flow cytometric analysis revealed that treatment induced apoptosis in AGS cells, with 30.4% apoptotic cells observed at 200 µg/mL. Consistently, mRNA and protein expression levels confirmed apoptosis cell death, as evidenced by an increased Bax/Bcl-2 ratio and elevated levels of cleaved caspase-9. Additionally, Western blot analysis revealed that treatment with higher doses of MM37-S-GNPs significantly downregulated the expression of ABCG1 and ABCG2 transporters. MM37-S-GNPs selectivelyeliminated gastric cancer cells through ROS-mediated mitochondrial damage and apoptotic pathways, while effectively regulating ABCG transporter expression, highlighting their potential as a promising nanotherapeutic agent.© 2026. 1940-087X2362026Oct16Journal of visualized experiments : JoVEJ Vis ExpDanshen Injection for 5-Fluorouracil-Resistant Gastric Cancer: Mitochondrial Apoptosis and Enhanced Drug Activity.10.3791/72391Gastric cancer ranks among the leading causes of cancer-related death worldwide, and the progressive emergence of 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) resistance represents a critical barrier to the efficacy of conventional chemotherapy, particularly 5-FU-based regimens. Danshen injection (DI), a clinically approved intravenous preparation derived from Salvia miltiorrhiza, has demonstrated preliminary antineoplastic activity; however, the mechanistic basis underlying its reversal of 5-FU resistance in gastric cancer has not been systematically defined. This study aimed to evaluate the antitumor efficacy of DI and its potential for enhanced combined activity with 5-FU in human gastric cancer cell lines (SGC7901 and BGC823), their 5-FU-resistant variants, and a xenograft mouse model. DI significantly induced apoptosis in both parental and drug-resistant cell lines, while CCK-8 assays confirmed markedly elevated IC50 values in resistant variants, validating the chemoresistant phenotype. The combination of DI and 5-FU produced enhanced antitumor effects superior to either agent alone, as demonstrated by increased apoptotic rates, upregulated expression of cleaved PARP and cleaved caspase-3, impaired mitochondrial membrane potential by JC-10 assay, and reduced colony formation. Mechanistically, DI promoted cytochrome c translocation from mitochondria to the cytoplasm, and elevated cleaved caspase-9 levels, effects that were further amplified upon co-treatment with 5-FU. Consistent antitumor activity was validated in vivo, with the combination regimen demonstrating superior tumor suppression compared with monotherapy. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that DI exerts meaningful antitumor activity and produces a greater combined effect with 5-FU in 5-FU-resistant gastric cancer. 2379-36942026Oct16ACS sensorsACS SensDielectrophoresis-Assisted PVDF/DES/Au NP-Based Microfluidic ECL Biosensor for In Situ Detection of Extracellular Vesicles.10.1021/acssensors.6c01896Herein, a regenerable dielectrophoresis (DEP)-assisted microfluidic electrochemiluminescence (ECL) biosensor was developed for in situ detection of extracellular vesicles (EVs) in gastric cancer ascites. In the integrated microfluidic ECL sensor, a poly(vinylidene fluoride-co-hexafluoropropylene) (PVDF-HFP)/deep eutectic solvent (DES)/Au NP (PDES/Au NPs) self-supporting electrode was developed. The DES treatment increased the polar β-phase proportion in PVDF-HFP and improved its conductivity. Meanwhile, Au NPs deposited on the electrode surface amplified the ECL signal of Ru(bpy)32+/TPrA@SiO2 nanobeads through the localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR) effect and generated an inhomogeneous electric field distribution for EV capture. Due to the DEP effect, the polarized EVs migrated and enriched on the PDES/Au NP electrode surface. As a result, the isolation time of EVs was reduced from 120 to 30 min. Consequently, the sensing platform effectively captured and detected EVs in gastric cancer ascites. The detection range was 1.0 × 101.6-1.0 × 105.3 particles μL-1, and the limit of detection was 9 particles μL-1. Moreover, a regenerative strategy was designed by controllably cleaving Au-S bonds on the self-supporting electrode. 1573-49785312026Oct16Molecular biology reportsMol Biol RepIntegrated in silico and in vitro analysis identifies a co-expression pattern associated with cisplatin/5-FU treatment response and metastatic features in gastric cancer.173110.1007/s11033-026-12888-3Gastric cancer remains a major cause of cancer mortality worldwide, and treatment failure is frequently associated with chemotherapy resistance and metastatic progression. Although cisplatin and 5-fluorouracil are commonly used components of gastric cancer chemotherapy, the extent to which gene-miRNA expression patterns associated with treatment response overlap with metastatic features remains incompletely understood.We integrated transcriptomic analysis of pretreatment GSE14210 samples with STRING network analysis and target-centric miRNA prioritization. Prioritized genes and miRNAs were evaluated by qRT-PCR in metastatic versus non-metastatic gastric cancer tissues and in MKN-45 3D spheroids exposed to cisplatin/5-FU; one patient-derived spheroid model was included as a feasibility observation.Analysis of the pretreatment GSE14210 cohort identified 414 upregulated DEGs, including 63 highly connected hubs (degree ≥ 10); 21 of these were also upregulated in tumor-versus-normal GEPIA comparisons. In metastatic tissues, CXCL8, MMP9, STAT1, miR-17-5p, miR-24-3p, and miR-124-3p were significantly increased, whereas miR-145-5p was significantly decreased; CCL5 was not significantly different. In cisplatin/5-FU-treated MKN-45 spheroids, CXCL8, MMP9, STAT1, miR-17-5p, miR-24-3p, and miR-124-3p showed significant expression changes, whereas CCL5 and miR-145-5p did not. MKN-45 spheroids regrew after cyclic exposure, consistent with an adaptive drug-tolerant phenotype, whereas the single patient-derived model showed limited recovery.These findings identify context-dependent candidate co-expression patterns across metastatic tissues and chemotherapy-exposed 3D models. They do not establish a shared causal mechanism and require functional validation in independent cohorts and additional patient-derived models.© 2026. 2589-004229102026Oct16iScienceiScienceMechanistic insights into VSIR-mediated AXL regulation and gastric cancer proliferation.11758011758011758010.1016/j.isci.2026.117580Gastric cancer (GC) progression is frequently driven by complex tumor microenvironment signals. Here, our study identifies V-set immunoregulatory receptor (VSIR) as a key driver of GC progression via AXL regulation. High-throughput RNA sequencing demonstrated that VSIR overexpression potently induces AXL upregulation in response to lipopolysaccharide (LPS) stimulation. This finding was confirmed through both VSIR overexpression and knockdown experiments. Mechanistically, our data demonstrated that STAT3 directly contributes to AXL transcriptional upregulation. Crucially, VSIR not only enhances LPS induced STAT3 phosphorylation, thereby amplifying AXL transcription, but also interacts with the AXL protein to stabilize it, leading to sustained AXL signaling. Functionally, the VSIR-AXL axis drives GC proliferation; notably, AXL inhibition suppresses this tumorigenesis, while combined AXL and HER2 blockade synergistically abrogates tumor growth. 2374-24452026Oct15JAMA oncologyJAMA OncolNivolumab-Ipilimumab for Localized Microsatellite Instability-High Gastric/Gastroesophageal Junction Adenocarcinoma: The Phase 2 NEONIPIGA Nonrandomized Clinical Trial.e26416210.1001/jamaoncol.2026.4162Neoadjuvant nivolumab plus ipilimumab in localized deficient mismatch repair/microsatellite instability-high gastric or gastroesophageal junction (GEJ) adenocarcinoma was evaluated in the NEONIPIGA study. The primary end point of pathological complete response (pCR) was previously reported.To report long-term follow-up results and secondary end points, including event-free survival (EFS) and overall survival (OS), of the NEONIPIGA study.The NEONIPIGA study is a French, multicenter, single-arm, phase 2 nonrandomized clinical trial that included patients with histologically proven cT2-T4NXM0 deficient mismatch repair/microsatellite instability-high GEJ adenocarcinoma who were eligible for surgery. Patients were enrolled between October 23, 2019, and June 4, 2021, and the database was locked on November 13, 2025.Neoadjuvant nivolumab, 240 mg, every 2 weeks for 6 cycles plus ipilimumab, 1 mg/kg, every 6 weeks for 2 cycles, followed by surgery 5 weeks after the last nivolumab dose, and adjuvant nivolumab, 480 mg, every 4 weeks for 9 cycles.EFS and OS.A total of 32 patients (median [range] age, 65 [40-80] years; 8 [28%] female and 21 [72%] were male) were included: 16 (50%) with gastric cancer and 16 (50%) with GEJ cancer. Three patients did not undergo surgery (1 with metastatic disease and 2 who refused). Twenty-seven patients (84%) completed neoadjuvant therapy and 14 (44%) received all treatment as planned. Neoadjuvant and adjuvant therapy-related grade 3/4 adverse events occurred in 6 (19%) and 4 patients (17%), respectively. Median follow-up was 48.3 months (95% CI, 44.8-52.0 months). Among the 32 patients in the intention-to-treat population, 4-year OS was 84.1% (95% CI, 65.8%-93.0%). In the 31 patients eligible for surgery, 4-year EFS was 83.5% (95% CI, 64.8%-92.8%). One patient relapsed with cerebral metastases. Six deaths occurred: 2 related to gastric cancer or treatment (1 patient had postoperative complications and 1 cerebral metastases) and 4 unrelated. All patients who did not undergo surgery achieved a clinical complete response after immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy. One patient subsequently died of causes unrelated to their cancer. Overall, 17 of 29 patients (59%) achieved pCR on surgical specimen. Safety was previously reported, and no additional late toxic effects were observed.In this phase 2 nonrandomized clinical trial, the immunotherapy regimen evaluated was associated with sustained long-term survival, but no clear evidence of improved survival over outcomes reported in other studies evaluating surgery alone in this patient population was observed. The high pCR rates and durable responses observed may provide useful information for designing future clinical studies, including randomized trials investigating organ-preserving 1573-26142026Oct15Journal of clinical monitoring and computingJ Clin Monit ComputAlteration of sublingual microcirculation in anemic patients during gastric cancer surgery under goal-directed fluid therapy: a prospective cohort study.10.1007/s10877-026-01511-2Goal-directed fluid therapy (GDFT) relies primarily on macrocirculatory hemodynamic variables for optimizing fluid therapy. Patients undergoing gastric cancer surgery often present with anemia, which may impair microvascular endothelial function and tissue oxygenation. How preoperative anemia influences intraoperative sublingual microcirculation and macro- and micro-circulatory coherence under GDFT is not known. Patients undergoing open radical gastrectomy were divided into anemic and non‑anemic groups according to their hemoglobin (Hb) levels. All patients received GDFT guided by pulse pressure variation. Sublingual microcirculatory (microvascular flow index [MFI], proportion of perfused vessels [PPV], total and perfused vessel density) and macrocirculatory (cardiac index [CI] and mean arterial pressure [MAP]) variables were measured before (T0) and immediately after induction of general anesthesia (T1), after tumor resection (T2) and at the end of surgery (T3). Mixed linear models were used to compare intergroup differences in sublingual microcirculation over time, and to analyze the correlations between macro- and micro-circulatory variables. Correlations between preoperative Hb and changes in MFI from each intraoperative time point to T0 were additionally assessed. A total of 49 patients were analyzed in present study. MFI showed a significant group‑by‑time interaction between the two groups (P = 0.030). In anemic patients (n = 22), MFI was significantly lower than that in non‑anemic patients (n = 27) at T1 (P = 0.013), and between-group differences were no longer evident at T3 (P = 0.461) under GDFT, although MFI remained below baseline in both groups. PPV was lower in anemic patients at T2 (P = 0.010). Correlation analyses demonstrated that lower preoperative Hb levels were associated with greater reductions in ΔMFI from T1 to T0 (Pearson's r = 0.343, P = 0.016) and T2 to T0 (Spearman's ρ = 0.369, P = 0.009). No significant associations were found between macro- and micro-circulatory variables in either group. Under GDFT, anemic patients exhibited greater perioperative alterations in sublingual microcirculation, particularly after anesthesia induction and tumor resection. Lower preoperative Hb concentrations were associated with greater reductions in MFI. Further, the lack of detectable associations between macrocirculatory and sublingual microcirculatory variables suggests that conventional hemodynamic targets may not fully reflect sublingual microvascular perfusion in this vulnerable population.Trial registration number: NCT07583927.© 2026. 1440-17462026Oct15Journal of gastroenterology and hepatologyJ Gastroenterol HepatolImpact of AI-Assisted Endoscopy on Secondary Review and Referral Decisions in Gastric Cancer Screening: A Multicenter Real-World Study.10.1111/jgh.70823Artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted endoscopy may support gastric cancer screening, but its impact on structured secondary human review remains unclear. We evaluated secondary review modifications and referral decisions before and after AI implementation.This retrospective multicenter study included 5013 screening esophagogastroduodenoscopy examinations performed before (n = 2021) and after (n = 2992) AI implementation. The primary outcome was secondary review modifications. Secondary outcomes included referral for further diagnostic evaluation. Multivariable logistic regression analyses adjusted for age, sex, Helicobacter pylori eradication status, prior-year endoscopy, and endoscopist experience were performed. Interaction analyses according to endoscopist experience and inverse probability of treatment weighting analyses were conducted. No external reference standard was available to verify secondary-review modifications or referral decisions.Secondary review modifications increased from 1.2% in the pre-AI period to 3.7% in the AI period (p < 0.01). A significant interaction was observed between AI implementation and endoscopist experience (p for interaction < 0.01), with increased modifications primarily among nonexpert endoscopists. Cancer-related modifications remained uncommon but increased after AI implementation (0.6% vs. 0.2%, p = 0.04). Referral rates decreased from 4.9% to 2.8% (p < 0.01), and AI implementation was independently associated with lower odds of referral (adjusted OR = 0.53; 95% confidence interval = 0.36-0.77).AI-assisted endoscopy was associated with lower referral rates; however, secondary review modifications persisted after AI implementation, particularly among nonexpert endoscopists. 1097-0142132202026Oct15CancerCancerDynamic changes of claudin 18.2 expression after systemic therapy in gastric and esophagogastric junction cancer.e70632e7063210.1002/cncr.70632Claudin 18.2 (CLDN18.2) is a promising therapeutic target in gastric/esophagogastric junction adenocarcinoma (GC/EGJC), but its dynamic expression during systemic therapy is unclear.CLDN18.2 expression by immunohistochemistry in paired tumor samples from 155 patients with advanced GC/EGJC was retrospectively evaluated before and after systemic therapy. CLDN18.2-positive was defined as ≥75% of viable tumor cells exhibiting moderate-to-strong (2+ or 3+) membranous staining.Among all patients, 54 (34.84%) were CLDN18.2-positive. Following treatment, the proportion of CLDN18.2-positive patients increased significantly to 61 (39.35%) (p < .001). Among patients who were CLDN18.2-negative at baseline, 57 (56.44%) showed increased expression after treatment, including 22 (21.78%) who converted to positive status. In contrast, among those CLDN18.2-positive at baseline, expression decreased in 35 patients (64.81%), with 15 (27.78%) converting to negative status (p < .001). Among patients receiving chemotherapy alone (n = 25), 1 (4.00%) converted to negative and 5 (20.00%) converted to positive, whereas among those receiving chemotherapy combined with immunotherapy (n = 130), 14 (10.77%) converted to negative and 17 (13.08%) converted to positive (p = .45). A total of 131 patients (84.52%) demonstrated changes in CLDN18.2 expression following therapy, encompassing both conversions across the positivity threshold and fluctuations within the same classification.CLDN18.2 expression in GC/EGJC is dynamic and frequently altered after systemic therapy. These findings support reassessment of CLDN18.2 status before initiating CLDN18.2-targeted therapies.© 2026 American Cancer Society. 1530-686040192026Oct15FASEB journal : official publication of the Federation of American Societies for Experimental BiologyFASEB JMethylmalonic Acid Induces Oxaliplatin Resistance Through Promoting DNA Damage Repair via the ATM/ATR Pathway in Gastric Cancer.e72332e7233210.1096/fj.202600528RSurgical intervention and chemotherapy have enhanced the survival rates of patients with advanced gastric cancer. However, the development of chemotherapy resistance remains a major obstacle to effective treatment, leading to poor prognosis in these patients. Increasing evidence suggests that metabolic alterations play crucial roles in mediating chemoresistance. Here we investigate the effects of methylmalonic acid (MMA), a mitochondrial-derived metabolite, on GC progression and oxaliplatin resistance. Analysis of clinical samples revealed that elevated serum MMA levels correlated with chemoresistance and advanced tumor stage in GC patients. Functional assays identified that MMA promoted GC cell proliferation, migration, and resistance to oxaliplatin by attenuating DNA damage. Mechanistically, MMA suppressed oxaliplatin-induced γH2AX expression while upregulating ATAD5 and activating the ATM/ATR-mediated homologous recombination (HR) repair pathway. In vivo studies further confirmed that MMA impaired the antitumor efficacy of oxaliplatin, while silencing PCCA, a key enzyme in MMA synthesis, or supplementing vitamin B12, a regulator of MMA metabolism, reversed MMA-induced chemoresistance. These findings highlight MMA as a potential indicator for oxaliplatin resistance and a therapeutic target in GC. Therefore, targeting MMA through vitamin B12 supplementation could serve as a promising therapeutic strategy to overcome chemoresistance in GC patients with elevated MMA levels.© 2026 Federation of 1090-21201822026Oct15Bioorganic chemistryBioorg ChemSolasonine inhibits growth of gastric cancer by targeting FTL-mediated ferroptosis.11057111057110.1016/j.bioorg.2026.110571S0045-2068(26)01107-7Solasonine (SS), a principal bioactive constituent of Solanum nigrum L., has attracted considerable attention due to its pronounced cytotoxic effects on cancer cells. Nevertheless, the precise mechanism of SS against gastric cancer remains inadequately explored. In this study, the therapeutic effects and potential targets of SS against gastric cancer were investigated. The results showed that SS markedly inhibited cell proliferation and promoted cell death in gastric cancer cells. Pharmacological inhibition studies revealed that the antitumor effects of SS predominantly rely on ferroptosis rather than apoptosis, necroptosis, or autophagy. This was corroborated by dysregulation of ferroptosis-related molecular markers, increased intracellular lipid peroxidation (LPO), malondialdehyde (MDA), and Fe2+ levels, and depletion of glutathione (GSH). Proteomic profiling identified ferritin light chain (FTL) as a putative target of SS, which was further supported by molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation, surface plasmon resonance (SPR), cellular thermal shift assay (CETSA), and western blot. Bioinformatics analyses demonstrated that FTL expression is significantly elevated at both the mRNA and protein levels in gastric cancer tissues. Higher FTL expression correlates with poorer overall survival. Overexpression of FTL in gastric cancer cells promoted the proliferation and mitigated SS-induced ferroptosis. In mice, SS treatment significantly inhibited tumor growth, suppressed FTL protein expression, and induced ferroptosis in gastric cancer xenografts. And the above effects can be rescued by application of a ferroptosis inhibitor. The antitumor activity and ferroptosis induction by SS were further validated using human organoid models. These findings demonstrate that SS inhibits gastric cancer growth by direct binding to FTL and promoting FTL-mediated ferroptosis. This mechanistic insight underscores the clinical applicability of SS for gastric cancer treatment.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier Inc. 1558-8238136202026Oct15The Journal of clinical investigationJ Clin InvestTumor NLRP3 amplification promotes immunotherapy resistance by inhibiting STAT1 signaling and MHC class I expression.e20181610.1172/JCI201816Immunotherapy resistance remains a challenge in immuno-oncology, and predictive biomarkers are needed to guide combination immunotherapy selection for the individual patient. We showed that elevated tumor-intrinsic NOD-, LRR-, and pyrin domain-containing protein 3 (NLRP3) signaling activity correlates with checkpoint inhibitor resistance in several independent cohorts of stage III/IV melanoma and gastroesophageal (GE) adenocarcinoma. In situ hybridization demonstrated tumor NLRP3 copy number gain in immunotherapy-resistant melanomas and GE adenocarcinomas harboring enhanced NLRP3 signaling activity. Nlrp3 amplification suppressed NOD-, LRR-, and CARD-containing 5-mediated (NLRC5-mediated) MHC class I upregulation, while spatial transcriptomic analysis of patient-derived GE adenocarcinomas confirmed that NLRP3 signaling activity inversely correlated with NLRC5 and MHC class I-associated gene expression. Mechanistically, NLRP3 binds to and inhibits signal transducer and activator of transcription 1 (STAT1) dimerization, nuclear translocation, and NLRC5 transcription. Consistent with these findings, pharmacologic inhibition of the NLRP3 inflammasome augmented tumor STAT1/NLRC5 signaling, enhanced MHC class I surface expression, and overcame anti-programmed cell death 1 resistance in an orthotopic model of gastric adenocarcinoma. This work reveals a fundamental link between cellular stress and tumor-mediated immune evasion and indicates that the tumor NLRP3 signaling pathway merits further clinical study as a therapeutic 1097-023140192026Oct15Rapid communications in mass spectrometry : RCMRapid Commun Mass SpectromLC-MS/MS-Based Phytochemical Characterization of Cakile maritima Methanol Extract and Its Photodynamic Anticancer Activity in Gastric Cancer Cells.e70143e70143e7014310.1002/rcm.70143In this study, the phytochemical composition, in vitro anticancer activity, photodynamic therapy (PDT) activity, and molecular interaction potential with carbonic anhydrase IX (CA IX) of Cakile maritima methanol extract were evaluated.LC-MS/MS analysis identified 11 compounds among 35 screened phytochemicals, with fumaric acid (13797.19 ppb), ferulic acid (771.37 ppb) and p-coumaric acid (601.95 ppb) accounting for approximately 97% of the total content. Molecular docking results demonstrated that sinapic acid (-6.13 kcal/mol) and quinic acid (-6.11 kcal/mol) exhibited the highest binding affinities toward CA IX. Cell culture studies revealed that LogIC50 values differed significantly among cell lines (p < 0.0001). PDT applied to the MKN-28 gastric cancer cell line significantly enhanced cytotoxicity compared with the control group, with the highest photodynamic efficacy observed under green-light irradiation (p < 0.0001).These findings indicate that C. maritima methanol extract exhibits light-enhanced cytotoxicity in MKN-28 gastric cancer cells and warrant further investigation regarding its potential photosensitising properties.© 2026 John Wiley & Sons Ltd.CaliskanSercin OzlemSO0000-0001-8464-5487Faculty of Medicine, Department of Biophysics, Usak University, Usak, Turkey.CaliskanMetinMFaculty of Medicine, Department of Medical Biology, Usak University, Usak, Turkey.TorunoğluEmine İncilayEİ0000-0003-4641-0067Faculty of Medicine, Department of Medical Biochemistry, Necmettin Erbakan University, Konya, Türkiye.DurmazAlperA0000-0001-6927-3283Ali Nihat Gökyiğit Botanical Garden Application and Research Center, Artvin Coruh University, Artvin, Türkiye.GümrükçüoğluAbidinAMedicinal-Aromatic Plants Application and Research Center, Artvin Çoruh University, Artvin, Türkiye.AytarErdi CanEC0000-0001-6045-0183Faculty of Agriculture, Department of Horticulture, Usak University, Usak, Turkey.engJournal Article

1532-21575312026Oct14European journal of surgical oncology : the journal of the European Society of Surgical Oncology and the British Association of Surgical OncologyEur J Surg OncolDevelopment and validation of an explainable model for predicting lymph node metastasis in early gastric cancer: a multicenter retrospective study with external and prospective validation.11231011231010.1016/j.ejso.2026.112310S0748-7983(26)00929-7Accurate preoperative prediction of lymph node metastasis (LNM) is essential for treatment selection in early gastric cancer (EGC), particularly when considering endoscopic submucosal dissection. Existing approaches show limited sensitivity for metastatic disease and frequently lack external or prospective validation. We aimed to develop and validate an interpretable machine-learning model for individualized preoperative prediction of LNM in EGC.In this multicenter study, four cohorts from three tertiary centers were included. Patients with pathologically confirmed EGC who underwent gastrectomy with lymph node dissection were retrospectively enrolled for training and external validation. A temporally independent cohort (September 2023-December 2024) was prospectively enrolled for validation. A preoperative pathology validation cohort (January 2025-January 2026) was also analyzed. Clinicopathological variables were selected using LASSO regression. SMOTE was applied to address class imbalance. Six machine-learning algorithms were compared. Model performance was assessed using AUC and PR-AUC, and interpretability was evaluated using SHapley Additive exPlanations. A web-based calculator was developed.Among 3412 patients in the training cohort, 467 (13.7%) had LNM. XGBoost achieved the best discrimination (training AUC = 0.9289) and maintained robust performance in the external (AUC = 0.8583; PR-AUC = 0.6079) and prospective validation cohorts (AUC = 0.8766; PR-AUC = 0.5137). In the preoperative pathology validation cohort, the model achieved an AUC of 0.8653 and a PR-AUC of 0.6050. Key predictors included lymphovascular/neural invasion, invasion depth, tumor location, differentiation, and tumor size.This externally and prospectively validated, interpretable machine-learning model provides transparent individualized risk estimates and may support personalized decision-making between endoscopic and surgical management in EGC.Copyright © 2026 Elsevier Ltd, BASO ~ The Association for Cancer Surgery, and the European Society of Surgical Oncology. 1532-21575312026Oct14European journal of surgical oncology : the journal of the European Society of Surgical Oncology and the British Association of Surgical OncologyEur J Surg OncolAn integrated pathological-radiological downstaging score for prognostic classification in gastric cancer after neoadjuvant chemotherapy: A multicenter retrospective study.11230811230810.1016/j.ejso.2026.112308S0748-7983(26)00927-3Neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC) followed by surgery is the standard treatment for locally advanced gastric cancer (LAGC). However, post-therapy staging based on ypTNM mainly reflects residual pathological status and does not capture pretreatment disease burden or the extent of tumor regression after NAC, limiting postoperative prognostic stratification. To address this limitation, we developed a Pathological-Radiological Integrated Model (PRIM) that combines baseline stage, post-treatment pathology, and radiologic response.We enrolled 414 patients with LAGC who underwent radical gastrectomy after NAC, including 348 in a development cohort and 66 in an external validation cohort. A Down-stage System (DS) was constructed to quantify tumor stage changes after NAC by weighting cT/cN and ypT/ypN categories using multivariable Cox regression. DS was then combined with RECIST response to establish the PRIM system. Prognostic performance and clinical utility were evaluated and compared with conventional ypTNM staging.PRIM stratified patients into four distinct risk groups with significantly different 3-year overall survival rates (86.9%, 69.9%, 40.0%, 21.2%; P < 0.001). Compared with ypTNM, PRIM demonstrated improved prognostic performance, with a higher C-index (0.728 vs. 0.696, P < 0.001), AUC (0.775 vs. 0.731, P < 0.001), and better model fit (AIC: 1471.62 vs. 1509.33; BIC: 1474.61 vs. 1512.32). Risk reclassification was also improved (NRI 14.49%; IDI 8.9%). Time-dependent ROC analysis showed consistently higher predictive accuracy for PRIM over 5 years.By integrating pathological and radiological response information, the PRIM classification provides improved postoperative prognostic stratification compared with ypTNM alone in patients with LAGC treated with NAC.Copyright © 2026. 1521-37732026Oct14Angewandte Chemie (International ed. in English)Angew Chem Int Ed EnglMetal-Center-Controlled Fenton-Like Reactivity of Biomimetic First-Row Transition Metal Complexes in Aqueous Anticancer Catalysis.e3481625e348162510.1002/anie.3481625Catalytic oxidative cancer therapy exploits elevated hydrogen peroxide levels within tumor microenvironments to induce selective oxidative damage in malignant cells. However, many ROS-generating therapeutic systems rely on heavy metals or structurally complex inorganic architectures, limiting their biological compatibility and catalytic selectivity. Inspired by nonheme iron-mediated redox catalysis, we report a series of water-soluble biomimetic first-row transition metal complexes supported by a picolylamine-derived nonheme ligand scaffold bearing a pendant hydroxyl group. Systematic variation of the metal center (Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, and Zn) generated divergent electrochemical behavior and distinct peroxide-activation reactivity, yet only the iron complex, [Fe(N2Py3OH)]2+ (1-Fe), promoted hydroxyl radical formation via Fenton-like hydrogen peroxide activation in water. Spectroscopic, electrochemical, and crystallographic analyses revealed a biomimetic coordination environment that stabilizes a quasi-reversible Fe(II)/Fe(III) redox couple suited to catalytic peroxide activation. In gastric cancer cells, 1-Fe induced intracellular oxidative stress, mitochondrial depolarization, lipid peroxidation, and concomitant apoptosis and ferroptosis, while exhibiting negligible toxicity toward normal fibroblasts. In combination with paclitaxel, 1-Fe produced synergistic antiproliferative activity in vitro and suppressed peritoneal tumor dissemination in vivo without overt systemic toxicity. Collectively, these results establish biomimetic iron complexes as molecular platforms for Fenton-like oxidative catalysis in redox-based cancer therapy.© 2026 Wiley‐VCH GmbH.ParkHyungbinHDepartment 2198-38442026Oct14Advanced science (Weinheim, Baden-Wurttemberg, Germany)Adv Sci (Weinh)DeepLNM: A Multimodal Model for Predicting Lymph Node Metastasis in Colorectal Cancer.e77860e77860e7786010.1002/advs.77860Accurate assessment of lymph node metastasis (LNM) is critical for prognostic stratification and treatment selection in colorectal cancer (CRC), yet imaging and routine pathology can yield false-negative/false-positive results. We propose DeepLNM, a multi-center foundation model for LNM prediction in CRC, evaluated with retrospective, external, prospective, and user study evidence. A multimodal dataset was assembled from three hospitals, with matched hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained whole-slide images (WSI), CT scans, and text. DeepLNM achieved a mean AUC of 0.922 in the internal cohort and AUCs of 0.872 and 0.848 in two external cohorts. In a prospective cohort from a registered clinical trial (NCT07239063), DeepLNM remained robust (AUC = 0.845). In a user study, DeepLNM improved diagnostic accuracy, especially for junior pathologists (95.0%-97.3%), while reducing diagnostic time and increasing confidence. To explore the model's generalizability, it was further validated in a gastric cancer cohort, achieving an AUC of 0.793. Finally, DeepLNM identified histopathological features associated with LNM, addressing the "black-box" concern of deep learning. Together, these results position DeepLNM as a clinically preliminarily validated multimodal model for predicting LNM status in CRC, potentially facilitating the clinical translation of AI pathology.© 2026 The Author(s). 1934-606934102026Oct14Cell host & microbeCell Host MicrobeA microbial chromatin remodeler drives gastric cancer progression and immune evasion by reprogramming the host epigenome.19301947.e81930-1947.e810.1016/j.chom.2026.08.011S1931-3128(26)00353-7First-line treatment for gastric cancer (GC) includes PD-1 blockade with chemotherapy, but resistance challenges treatment success. We identify Streptococcus anginosus (SA) as a tumor-resident oncobacterium driving GC progression and immune evasion. SA is enriched in GC patient tumors and drives tumor growth in mice. SA extracellular vesicles (saEVs) translocate the bacterial chromatin remodeler saSNF2 into host cells. saSNF2 partners with host transcription factor TEAD1-through its ATPase activity and participation in BRG1/BRM-associated factor (BAF) complex assembly-to activate oncogenic transcription. This transkingdom interaction upregulates the palmitoyltransferase ZDHHC11, which stabilizes PD-L1 via palmitoylation to establish an immunosuppressive niche, while amplifying other TEAD1 target genes to fuel tumor progression. saEVs promote tumor growth and limit CD8+ T cell infiltration in vivo. Pharmacological inhibition of ZDHHC11 reverses immune evasion and synergizes with anti-PD-1 checkpoint blockade. These findings establish SA as a multifaceted driver of GC and highlight the saSNF2-ZDHHC11 axis as a target to potentiate immunotherapy.Copyright © 2026 The Author(s). Published by Elsevier Inc. 2391-54632112026JanOpen medicine (Warsaw, Poland)Open Med (Wars)Postoperative malnutrition predicts severe chemotherapy toxicity after gastrectomy: evaluation of an inflammation-anemia phenotype.20261550202615502026155010.1515/med-2026-1550Severe toxicity during adjuvant chemotherapy after curative gastrectomy is common. We evaluated whether postoperative malnutrition predicts severe toxicity, whether an inflammation-anemia (IA) composite adds incremental information, and whether a simple risk model offers clinical utility.In this single-center prospective cohort, adults received adjuvant chemotherapy after curative gastrectomy. Malnutrition was defined as albumin <35 g/L, BMI <18.5 kg/m2, or low skeletal muscle index; IA as CRP ≥1.5 mg/L plus hemoglobin <120 g/L. A ridge-penalized logistic model included age, pathologic stage, regimen (S-1 vs. oxaliplatin-based multi-agent), malnutrition, IA, and a malnutrition × regimen interaction. Nested 5-fold cross-validation and decision curve analysis evaluated model performance and net benefit.Of 222 screened patients, 219 were analyzed. Severe toxicity occurred in 48/219 (21.9 %), more often with multi-agent therapy than S-1 (23.5 vs. 8.7 %). Malnutrition was strongly associated with toxicity and remained an independent predictor (penalized OR 3.42, 95 % CI 1.75-6.68), whereas IA was not. Out-of-sample AUROC was 0.695, Brier score 0.156, and calibration slope 0.86. At a 0.30 threshold, net benefit was higher for the full model than for base + malnutrition.Postoperative malnutrition is a key predictor of severe adjuvant chemotherapy toxicity after gastrectomy. 2666-63402026Oct13Med (New York, N.Y.)MedEarly detection of gastric cancer using DNA features in red blood cells, with multicenter validation.10132510132510.1016/j.medj.2026.101325S2666-6340(26)00328-4Early detection of gastric cancer (GC) is limited by invasive endoscopy and poor sensitivity of blood-based biomarkers. Red blood cells (RBCs), the most abundant cells in the circulation, are anucleate but can retain DNA remnants that have been associated with pathological stress. Here, we report a non-invasive strategy for GC detection based on genome-wide profiling of DNA remnants retained in RBCs (rbcDNA).We performed shallow whole-genome sequencing of rbcDNA from 1-2 mL of peripheral blood of 865 individuals, including 434 treatment-naive GC patients and 431 non-GC controls with benign gastric conditions. In the discovery cohort, we identified 1,000 reproducible rbcDNA read-depth features distinguishing GC from non-cancer states. A machine learning classifier based on dimensionally reduced GC-associated rbcDNA features was trained in the discovery cohort (n = 435), with the cutoff fixed at 90% specificity, and evaluated in a test cohort (n = 109) and three independent multicenter validation cohorts (n = 321).The classifier achieved the areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUCs) of 84% in nested cross-validation of the discovery cohort and 95% in the test cohort. The disease varies by region, histology, metastatic site, and treatment history. It also develops within a gastric niche shaped by acid, mucus, polarity, microbes, and stroma. Patient-derived organoids (PDOs) can preserve tumor-linked epithelial states and support living biobanks. They also enable genotype-phenotype studies and functional testing of therapeutic vulnerabilities. Their clinical value depends on representation, not model complexity alone. The assay must also return clear results within a useful clinical window. This review evaluates GC PDOs as functional companion models for precision oncology rather than stand-alone treatment decision tools. We discuss four barriers that limit clinical readiness. Establishment bias reduces representation of diffuse-type, scirrhous, and signet-ring cell carcinomas. Standard organoid lumens do not reproduce gastric acidity, stratified mucus, or Helicobacter pylori-driven polarity loss. Long-term expansion can select culture-adapted clones and weaken clinical representativeness. PDO drug screening also remains difficult to align with urgent treatment timelines. Fresh-sample assays may shorten turnaround time but reduce scale and depth. We further highlight biological insights gained from GC organoids. These include niche independence, epigenetic dependencies, ARID1A-linked vulnerabilities, and chemotherapy resistance. We propose a readiness framework based on six criteria: tumor authenticity, subtype coverage, niche fidelity, turnaround time, assay standards, and outcome validation. Future Oncol 17(31):4081–4089. https://doi.org/10.2217/fon-2021-0632 (in eng)10.2217/fon-2021-06323426906720301318NBK1139University of Washington, SeattleSeattle (WA)GeneReviews®199319932026AdamMargaret PMPBickSarahSMirzaaGhayda MGMWallaceStephanie ESEAmemiyaAnneAInternetDiffuse Gastric and Lobular Breast Cancer SyndromeengBarbosa-MatosRitaRi3S - Instituto de Investigação e Inovação em Saúde, University of Porto, Porto, PortugalCórdovaLilianLDepartment of Medical Genetics, University of British Columbia, Vancouver, CanadaSchraderKasmintanKProgram Medical Co-Director, Hereditary Cancer, BC Cancer;, Assistant Professor, Department of Medical Genetics, University of British Columbia, Vancouver, CanadaOliveiraCarlaCi3S - Instituto de Investigação e Inovação em Saúde;, Institute of Molecular Pathology and Immunology;, Faculty of Medicine, University of Porto, Porto, PortugalReviewDiffuse gastric and lobular breast cancer syndrome (DGLBCS) is associated with an increased risk, in males and females, of diffuse gastric cancer (DGC), a poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma (also referred to as signet ring cell carcinoma or isolated cell-type carcinoma) that infiltrates into the stomach wall, causing thickening of the wall (linitis plastica) without forming a distinct mass. In females with CDH1-related DGLBCS, but not in males, there is also an increased risk for lobular breast cancer (LBC), characterized by small, non-cohesive cells dispersed in the stroma or arranged in single-file infiltrating patterns. Cleft lip with or without cleft palate has also been reported in some individuals with CDH1-related DGLBCS.The diagnosis of DGLBCS can be established in an individual with suggestive findings and a germline heterozygous pathogenic variant in CDH1 or a germline heterozygous truncating pathogenic variant in CTNNA1 identified by molecular genetic testing. Affected individuals from families that meet consensus genetic testing criteria for DGLBCS who do not have an identified pathogenic variant in CDH1 or CTNNA1 have suspected DGLBCS of unknown genetic cause (also referred to as hereditary diffuse gastric cancer [HDGC]-like).Targeted therapy: Prophylactic gastrectomy for diffuse gastric cancer is an option from early adulthood in individuals with normal endoscopy / gastric biopsies and a DGLBCS-related CDH1 pathogenic variant regardless of family history or a DGLBCS-related CTNNA1 pathogenic variant and a family history of DGC and/or LBC. Supportive care: Management of DGLBCS requires a multidisciplinary team. Standard treatment to eradicate H pylori infection; total gastrectomy for early or advanced DGC; perioperative and/or adjuvant therapy for advanced DGC; surgery, hormonal therapy, and perioperative and/or adjuvant chemotherapy for LBC; consider risk-reducing contralateral mastectomy; standard treatments for cleft correction by craniofacial specialists. Surveillance: For individuals with CDH1- or CTNNA1-related DGLBCS, referral to a high-risk gastric screening program with a thorough ≥30-minute upper endoscopy with multiple targeted and random biopsies every six to 12 months beginning in early adulthood or five to ten years prior to the earliest gastric cancer diagnosis in the family. For females with CDH1-related DGLBCS or CTNNA1-related DGLBCS and personal or family history of breast cancer, referral to a high-risk breast cancer screening program with monthly self-breast exams beginning at age 20 years; annual clinical breast examinations, education on clinical features of breast cancer, and bilateral breast MRI with contrast from age 30 years; annual mammography between MRI screens from age 30-40 years; if MRI is unavailable, breast ultrasound should be combined with mammogram. In individuals with CDH1-related cleft lip/palate, annual audiology and speech evaluation throughout childhood. In individuals with suspected DGLBCS of unknown cause (also referred to as HDGC-like), referral to a high-risk gastric screening program with a thorough ≥30-minute upper endoscopy with multiple targeted and random biopsies annually beginning at age 40 years or ten years prior to the earliest gastric cancer diagnosis in the family; endoscopy interval can be increased after two consecutive normal biopsies at the discretion of the endoscopist. Referral to a high-risk breast cancer screening program; in those with a personal or family history of breast cancer of any type, monthly self-exams beginning at age 20 years, annual clinical breast exam and education of clinical features of breast cancer beginning at age 30 years; additional breast screening as recommended by high-risk breast cancer specialists. Evaluation of relatives at risk: Offer at-risk relatives of a proband with CDH1- or CTNNA1-related DGLBCS predictive testing for the familial pathogenic variant. This will allow identification of individuals who would benefit from intensive surveillance for early cancer detection and/or prophylactic surgeries targeting organs associated with DGLBCS. Offer first-degree relatives of a proband with suspected DGLBCS of unknown genetic cause (HDGC-like) surveillance tailored to the individual's personal and family history. Pregnancy management: Nutritional consequences of total gastrectomy should be discussed before and during pregnancy. Pregnancy should be delayed at least six to 12 months after total gastrectomy, to allow for weight stabilization and nutritional recovery.DGLBCS is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. The majority of individuals diagnosed with CDH1-related DGLBCS inherited the CDH1 pathogenic variant from a parent (because of reduced penetrance, the parent from whom the pathogenic variant was inherited may not have developed cancer). Some individuals diagnosed with CTNNA1-related DGLBCS have an affected first- or second-degree relative with gastric or breast cancer. Some individuals with DGLBCS have the disorder as the result of a de novo pathogenic variant. Each child of an individual with DGLBCS has a 50% chance of inheriting the DGLBCS-related pathogenic variant. 2211-124745102026Oct12Cell reportsCell RepEpCAM-dependent membrane mechanics regulate nuclear deformation and promote gastric cancer metastasis.11812611812610.1016/j.celrep.2026.118126S2211-1247(26)01205-2Diffuse gastric cancer is highly metastatic and lacks effective therapeutic targets. Using membrane proteomics, gastric cancer cell models, biophysical measurements, and in vivo metastasis assays, we identify EpCAM as a regulator of membrane-cytoskeletal mechanics. EpCAM overexpression was associated with reduced apparent plasma membrane tension, ERM-actin remodeling, increased traction forces, and nuclear deformation. Functional perturbation of ezrin and lamin A/C supported the involvement of membrane-cytoskeleton-nucleus mechanical coupling in confined migration. EpCAM knockout or monoclonal antibody blockade reduced tumor invasion and lymph node dissemination in vivo. These findings establish a mechanobiological framework linking EpCAM-dependent membrane mechanics to metastatic behavior and highlight EpCAM-associated mechanical regulation as a potential therapeutic vulnerability in diffuse gastric cancer.Copyright © 2026 The Authors. 1537-45132026Oct12Journal of immunotherapy (Hagerstown, Md. : 1997)J ImmunotherAssociation Between Neoadjuvant Immunochemotherapy Efficacy and Pathologic Characteristics in dMMR Gastric/Gastroesophageal Junction Adenocarcinoma.10.1097/CJI.0000000000000625Neoadjuvant immunotherapy (NAIC) is feasible and associated with a high rate of pathologic complete response (pCR) in deficient mismatch repair (dMMR)/microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H) gastric and gastroesophageal junction cancers (GC/GEJC). However, the association between NAIC efficacy and pathologic characteristics remains unclear. We conducted a retrospective study to evaluate this relationship. Patients with dMMR/MSI-H GC/GEJC who received neoadjuvant immunotherapy were included. The effects of different neoadjuvant regimens were compared, and pathologic characteristics were analyzed between tumor regression grade TRG1 and TRG2 groups. The χ2 test was used to estimate relative risks (RRs) with 95% CIs. In total, 39 patients with dMMR/MSI-H GC/GEJC who received neoadjuvant immunotherapy were included. All patients underwent complete R0 resection; 22 patients (56%) achieved pCR in both the primary tumor and lymph nodes. The chemotherapy plus immunotherapy group and the immunotherapy-only group achieved significantly higher TRG1 rates compared with the chemotherapy group (RR=4.2, 95% CI=1.5-15.0, P=0.0004; and RR=4.4, 95% CI=1.7-15.7, P=0.003, respectively). The intestinal subtype also demonstrated a higher TRG1 rate than the mixed subtype (RR=2.5, 95% CI=1.1-8.7, P=0.0196). Neoadjuvant immunotherapy achieved a high pCR rate in patients with dMMR/MSI-H locally advanced, resectable GC/GEJC relative to chemotherapy. The intestinal subtype may serve as a histologic biomarker of enhanced sensitivity to neoadjuvant immunotherapy in this patient population.Copyright © 2026 The Author(s). 2198-38442026Oct11Advanced science (Weinheim, Baden-Wurttemberg, Germany)Adv Sci (Weinh)Lactylation-Mediated HER2 Stabilization Promotes Trastuzumab Resistance in Gastric Cancer.e77955e77955e7795510.1002/advs.77955Trastuzumab is the standard first-line targeted therapy for human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-positive gastric cancer (GC). Unfortunately, its clinical efficacy is often compromised by the development of drug resistance. The Warburg effect, a hallmark of cancer metabolism, leads to substantial lactate accumulation. Nevertheless, the impact of metabolic reprogramming on the response to HER2-targeted therapy remains poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that AARS1-mediated lactylation of HER2 promotes trastuzumab resistance in GC. Mechanistically, lactylation at lysine 1171 (K1171) promotes USP11-mediated deubiquitination and stabilization of HER2 and also enhances the interaction between HER2 and EGFR. Clinically, elevated HER2 K1171 lactylation levels are associated with poor prognosis in GC patients. Inhibiting HER2 K1171 lactylation with L-alanine or stiripentol-a lactate dehydrogenase inhibitor (LDHi) clinically approved for epilepsy-significantly sensitizes tumor cells to trastuzumab. Furthermore, a cell-penetrating peptide designed to specifically block HER2 K1171 lactylation potently enhances antitumor efficacy in vivo. In summary, our findings identify HER2 lactylation as a critical mechanism underlying trastuzumab resistance and highlight lactate metabolism as a promising therapeutic target for HER2-positive GC.© 2026 The Author(s). 1178-6930192026OncoTargets and therapyOnco Targets TherEfficacy and Safety of Low-Dose Hypofractionated Radiotherapy Combined with Immunotherapy for Liver Metastases: A Single-Center Retrospective Analysis.62712462712462712410.2147/OTT.S627124To evaluate the efficacy and safety of low-dose hypofractionated radiotherapy (LDHRT) for liver metastases when combined with immunotherapy.Patients with liver metastases receiving immunotherapy were enrolled in this study at Changzhou Second People's Hospital from January 2019 to May 2025 (Ethics Approval No. [2021]KY117-01). LDHRT (12 Gy in 3 fractions) was administered to the liver metastases using volumetric modulated arc therapy (VMAT). The tumor response was evaluated according to the RECIST 1.1 standard. Clinical and imaging data were collected to assess changes in tumors inside and outside the radiation field before and after LDHRT, as well as the median progression-free survival (PFS) for lesions within the radiation field.A total of 51 patients were included, with the median age of 69 (range 47-84) years; 86.3% (44/51) were male, and 94.1% (48/51) had an ECOG performance status (PS) score ≥1. Additionally, 54.9% (28/51) had received ≥3 lines of prior therapy. Due to the continuous progression of liver metastases under systemic treatment, LDHRT was administered for the liver metastases. The study found a high local control rate within the radiation field as the objective response rate (ORR) and disease control rate (DCR) within the radiation field were 17.6% and 86.3%, respectively. However, the efficacy for lesions outside the radiation field was significantly inferior, with an ORR of 0% and a DCR of 35.3%. The median PFS for lesions within the radiation field was 4.23 months. Patients with colorectal liver metastases (CRLM) showed better PFS than those with gastric cancer liver metastases (GCLM). The most common adverse events were fatigue (16/51, 31.4%), abnormal liver function (11/51, 21.6%), and hypothyroidism (7/51, 13.7%). No patients discontinued treatment due to treatment-related adverse events.LDHRT combined with immunotherapy provided favorable local control and was generally well tolerated in patients with liver metastases. 1865-72652026Oct10Clinical journal of gastroenterologyClin J GastroenterolA case of recurrent early gastric cancer with a giant injection-related granuloma after endoscopic submucosal dissection resulting in non-curative resection.10.1007/s12328-026-02467-1A 69-year-old man underwent endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD) for early gastric cancer of the lower gastric body. The lateral margin was positive, corresponding to an eCura C-1 classification, and surveillance with upper gastrointestinal endoscopy every 6 months was performed. Local recurrence was detected 4 years later, and repeat ESD resulted in an eCura C-2 classification, prompting additional surgical resection. No lymph node metastasis was identified, and the patient remained recurrence-free for 11 months. Histopathological examination of the surgical specimen revealed extensive foreign body granuloma formation involving the deep muscularis propria and subserosal tissue. The granulomas were Alcian-blue positive, with staining intensity reduced after hyaluronidase treatment, suggesting the involvement of a hyaluronic acid-containing submucosal injection agent. No granulomas were observed in the repeat ESD specimen obtained 6 months before surgery. Inflammatory cell infiltration around the lymphatic vessels was observed, suggesting the involvement of lymphatic pathways to the gradual spread and extensive distribution of the granulomatous reaction over time. Submucosal injection-related granuloma formation after ESD is rare, but extensive granuloma formation may complicate the interpretation of post-ESD findings and potentially increase the technical difficulty of subsequent treatment. Clinicians should be aware of this possibility when performing surveillance and additional treatment after ESD.© 2026. 2576-20952026Oct09Animal models and experimental medicineAnimal Model Exp MedMolecular mechanism of Xanthotoxol against gastric cancer: A comprehensive study integrating network pharmacology, computer simulations, and experimental validation.10.1002/ame2.70234Gastric cancer (GC) is a prevalent malignant tumor of the digestive system worldwide. Xanthotoxol (Xan), a natural compound extracted from traditional Chinese medicine such as Angelica archangelica, has demonstrated antitumor properties. However, its specific effects on GC remain unreported.Hub targets of Xan in GC were identified by integrating weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) with network pharmacology. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were conducted to analyze the interaction between the hub targets and Xan. The effects of Xan on GC cell proliferation, cell cycle, apoptosis, migration, and invasion were examined using cell experiments and xenograft tumor model. Histopathological evaluation of changes in tumor and liver tissues was performed after Xan intervention. Western blot and reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) were employed to analyze hub target expression and clarify Xan's molecular mechanism against GC.A total of six hub genes highly correlated with GC were identified (MMP12, KDR, CCND1, PDGFRB, PLAU, and PLK1). Molecular docking and MD simulations revealed a significant binding affinity between Xan and hub genes. Experiments demonstrated that Xan inhibited proliferation, cell cycle, migration, and invasion while promoting apoptosis. Xan could alleviate liver injury caused by subcutaneous tumor in mice. Furthermore, Xan upregulated MMP12 expression and downregulated KDR, CCND1, PDGFRB, PLAU, and PLK1 in GC cells.Xan shows promise as a GC treatment by modulating MMP12, KDR, CCND1, PDGFRB, PLAU, and PLK1 expression, which inhibits proliferation, cell cycle, migration, and invasion, while enhancing apoptosis and reducing liver damage.© 2026 The Author(s).
