2468-2942492026Oct09Cancer treatment and research communicationsCancer Treat Res CommunThe prognostic value of HER2 in gastroesophageal adenocarcinoma - a meta-analysis.10145310145310.1016/j.ctarc.2026.101453S2468-2942(26)00363-1HER2 amplification and overexpression are predictive markers for HER2-targeted therapies in gastroesophageal adenocarcinoma. However, unlike in breast cancer, the prognostic significance of HER2 status in this disease remains uncertain, with conflicting evidence across studies.We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of studies reporting hazard ratios (HRs) for overall survival (OS) based on HER2 status, identified through PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science. Eligible studies included HER2-positive and HER2-negative patients with gastroesophageal adenocarcinoma, using IHC and/or ISH diagnostics. Pooled HRs were calculated using random-effects models. Subgroup analyses and meta-regressions were performed by stage, treatment, and covariates. A novel statistical framework was applied to contextualize HER2's prognostic role.Eighty studies encompassing 30,574 patients were included. HER2 positivity was associated with poorer OS in univariate analyses for stage I-III (HR 1.29, 95% CI: 1.02-1.61) and stage I-IV disease (HR 1.58, 95% CI: 1.14-2.20), and remained significant in multivariate analyses (HR 1.46 and HR 1.52, respectively). In metastatic disease, HER2 positivity was associated with poorer survival in untreated cohorts (multivariate HR 1.37, 95% CI: 1.01-1.85; p = 0.043), but with improved survival in trastuzumab-treated cohorts in univariate analysis (HR 0.73, 95% CI: 0.61-0.88; p = 0.0007) and borderline multivariate analysis (HR 0.71, 95% CI: 0.50-1.00; p = 0.047).HER2 positivity was independently associated with poorer overall survival in gastroesophageal adenocarcinoma. In metastatic disease, pooled estimates differed according to trastuzumab exposure, with more favorable outcomes observed in trastuzumab-treated HER2-positive cohorts. These findings support an adverse prognostic association of HER2 positivity and further investigation of HER2-directed therapy in earlier-stage disease.Copyright © 2026 The Authors. 1536-5964105412026Oct09MedicineMedicine (Baltimore)Analysis of a case of immune-related pancreatitis induced by anti-PD-1 antibody therapy for gastric cancer: A case report.e50285e50285e5028510.1097/MD.0000000000050285Immune-related pancreatitis is a rare but clinically significant adverse event associated with immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy. Early recognition and appropriate management are essential to prevent potentially serious outcomes. Herein, we report a case of suspected immune-related pancreatitis during nivolumab-based immunotherapy for metastatic gastric cancer.An 82-year-old female patient, post-gastrectomy for gastric cancer with subsequent cerebral metastases, multiple leptomeningeal metastases, subcutaneous metastases, and retroperitoneal lymph node metastases, received "nivolumab + apatinib" therapy for 4 cycles. On the second day of the fourth cycle of treatment, the patient developed mild epigastric pain, acid regurgitation, and elevated pancreatic enzyme levels, suggestive of immune-related pancreatitis. Alternative etiologies, including biliary disease, alcohol use, and hypertriglyceridemia, were excluded. The patient was classified as Grade 1 according to the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events v5.0 and was managed with fasting, parenteral nutrition, octreotide, enzyme inhibition, and electrolyte balance adjustment. Pancreatic enzyme levels normalized, and symptoms resolved. Nivolumab and apatinib were subsequently withheld.This case highlights that immune-related pancreatitis may present with only mild abdominal symptoms despite marked pancreatic enzyme elevation during immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy. Clinicians should maintain a high index of suspicion for pancreatic immune-related adverse events, even in the absence of typical imaging findings, and systematically exclude alternative causes to ensure timely and appropriate management.Copyright © 2026 the Author(s). 1536-5964105412026Oct09MedicineMedicine (Baltimore)Gastric cancer burden from 1990 to 2021, Joinpoint analysis, projections to 2036, and health inequality assessment: Findings from the Global Burden of Disease study 2021.e50967e50967e5096710.1097/MD.0000000000050967Gastric cancer (GC) remains a major global health issue with high incidence and mortality. This study evaluates the global burden and health disparities of GC from 1990 to 2021 and projects trends through 2036, providing evidence for targeted control measures. The data were sourced from the 2021 Global Burden of Disease study, covering the incidence, mortality, disability-adjusted life years, age-standardized incidence rate, age-standardized mortality rate, and age-standardized disability-adjusted life years rate of GC across 204 countries and regions from 1990 to 2021. Joinpoint regression analysis was employed to examine trends between 1990 and 2021, while a Bayesian age-period-cohort model was constructed to assess and project trends up to 2036. Concentration curves and concentration indices were used to examine cross-national relative inequalities in GC burden across sociodemographic index (SDI) levels. Compared to 1990, the number of GC cases and deaths increased in 2021; meanwhile, the age-standardized incidence rate, age-standardized mortality rate, and age-standardized disability-adjusted life years rate declined, respectively. Males consistently faced a higher disease burden across all age groups. The gap between high-SDI and low-SDI countries is narrowing, with underdeveloped countries bearing a relatively heavier burden of stomach cancer. The Bayesian age-period-cohort model predicts a further decline in the global GC burden by 2036. GC remains a substantial global burden, affecting regions and countries worldwide with pronounced geographic, age, and sex-related disparities. Effective interventions - such as Helicobacter pylori prevention and treatment, as well as widespread early GC screening - are crucial for reducing incidence risks and improving survival outcomes.Copyright © 2026 the Author(s). 2516-02302026Oct08Nanoscale advancesNanoscale AdvBiomaterial-driven remove-remodel-repair (3R) strategy for full-cycle gastric cancer management: bibliometric mapping, preclinical evidence, and a translational roadmap.10.1039/d6na00583gGastric cancer (GC) remains a leading cause of cancer mortality worldwide and is characterized by prolonged precancerous progression, dynamic tumor-immune-microbiota interactions, and treatment-associated toxicity that can compromise host defense and tissue recovery. These features create a clinical need for full-cycle management spanning prevention, early eradication, advanced therapy, and postoperative rehabilitation. Here, we propose a biomaterial-driven 3R framework for GC management across the disease continuum, comprising remove for lesion clearance, remodel for immune microenvironment regulation, and repair for tissue restoration. A bibliometric analysis of 1559 publications maps the evolution of biomaterial-enabled GC research and provides an evidence landscape for this framework. Representative nanomaterials, biomimetic hydrogels, engineered microbial carriers, and regenerative matrices are mapped to clinical needs across prevention, endoscopic and perioperative intervention, systemic therapy, and rehabilitation. The 3R occupy distinct translational tiers: remove- and remodel-oriented platforms are predominantly supported by mechanistic preclinical studies, whereas selected repair-oriented materials, including endoscopic hemostatic, sealing, and submucosal-support platforms, already have human clinical evidence. 1432-22182026Oct08Surgical endoscopySurg EndoscIndocyanine green-guided lymphadenectomy and survival of patients with gastric cancer: a systematic review and meta-analysis of time-to-event data.10.1007/s00464-026-13324-0Indocyanine green fluorescence imaging (ICG-FI) is increasingly used for lymph node mapping in gastric cancer (GC) surgery, but its impact on long-term oncologic outcomes remains unclear. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the long-term survival benefits of ICG-guided lymphadenectomy compared with conventional surgery.PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Library were searched from inception to November 2025, supplemented by clinical trial registries. Studies comparing ICG-guided versus non-ICG-guided lymphadenectomy in GC patients were included. Primary outcomes were overall survival (OS) and disease-free survival (DFS). Secondary outcomes included lymph node yield and postoperative complications. Random-effects models were used, and Bayesian analyses estimated the probability of survival benefit.Seven studies comprising 7518 patients were included. ICG significantly improved 3-year OS (HR = 0.635, 95% CI 0.511-0.790, P = 0.000), 3-year DFS (HR = 0.682, 95% CI 0.530-0.877, P = 0.003), and 5-year OS (HR = 0.700, 95% CI 0.507-0.966, P = 0.030), with Bayesian posterior probabilities of 100%, 100%, and 99.1%, respectively. No significant differences were observed for 2-year OS or DFS. ICG significantly increased lymph node yield (WMD = 6.557, 95% C1 3.821-9.294, P = 0.000) without increasing postoperative complications (RR = 0.899, 95% CI 0.647-1.250, P = 0.527).ICG-guided lymphadenectomy is associated with improved long-term survival and increased lymph node dissection without increasing complications. These findings support ICG-FI as a valuable adjunct in gastric cancer surgery. Further high-quality randomized trials are warranted to validate these results in diverse populations and settings.CRD420261342420.© 2026.
